}",1582,0,1,1,"AmirX contains a series of typical “plumbing” errors that open it to theft, denial of service or accidental loss of funds.
• _defiSwap( ) performs wallet.call(…) first and only afterwards executes _feeDispersal( ).
• _buyBack( ) makes aggregator.call(…) immediately after granting the aggregator a fresh allowance.
• plugin.increaseClaimableBy(…) is another external call made while the contract still holds TELCOIN and other assets.
No re-entrancy guard is used, so any of those external contracts can call back into AmirX and repeat operations or drain freshly approved tokens.
2. Unlimited / lingering allowances to the aggregator
but never resets the allowance to 0 afterwards.
A malicious (or hacked) aggregator can pull every future token that is ever sent to AmirX, long after the swap has finished.
3. All msg.value is forwarded to the aggregator (POL branch)
The ETH/value attached to the *original* user transaction is blindly propagated to
• If the caller forgets to set value to 0, all native coins go to the aggregator.
• The contract itself never tracks nor validates how much ETH is really required for the swap.
4. Balance-difference arithmetic reverts with deflationary tokens
fBalance - iBalance is executed twice without checking that fBalance ≥ iBalance.
When the origin token is fee-on-transfer or burns on transfer, fBalance < iBalance and the entire swap reverts, enabling grief/DoS attacks.
wallet and walletData are user supplied.  Anyone holding SWAPPER_ROLE can make AmirX execute *any* call in the context of an arbitrary wallet contract.
Combined with the missing re-entrancy guard this is dangerous and can be chained with the unlimited allowance issue to steal funds.
6. Mis-use of the POL sentinel address
The address 0x…1010 is treated both as “native POL” and as an ERC-20 in different parts of the code (e.g. rescueCrypto).
If an ERC-20 really exists at that address on some chains the SUPPORT_ROLE can unintentionally drain native coins or get blocked by insufficient balance.
7. No minimum-return / slippage checks on swaps
Neither _buyBack( ) nor the higher-level swap functions verify how many tokens were actually obtained, opening the door to sandwich attacks or very unfavorable quotes.
Because every aggregator.call( ) is wrapped in require(success,…), a malfunctioning or malicious aggregator can permanently brick all swap flows that have to pass through it.
9. Lack of event emission for critical operations
Rescue, fee dispersal, and swap operations are silent, making incident response and auditing far harder.
Any one of (1)–(3) is enough to let an attacker with control over (or the ability to re-enter through) wallet / aggregator / plugin steal the entire token balance held by the contract.","---
### **[M-1] Burn Limit Can Be Violated in defiToStablecoinSwap**

The contract verifies the burn limit for an internal stablecoin swap *before* executing an external DeFi swap. However, the actual amount received from the external swap can differ due to slippage, and this new amount is not re-verified. This oversight can lead to a transaction that burns more of the stablecoin than is allowed by the protocol's minimum supply rules. This issue could result in violating the protocol's constraints and potentially destabilizing the stablecoin's supply.

This is a critical oversight in swap operations and is consistent with Solidity best practices, which recommend implementing slippage checks to ensure the integrity of token balances and prevent unfavorable outcomes.
